lines: Every clause this section covered answers one question at a time. Now a construct that looks at its neighbours on purpose, one window at a time.
Watch the bracket move down the four orders. An aggregate would collapse them into a single number. This does not.
Every order keeps its own row, and gets an answer computed from the rows around it.
The whole topic is one question: which neighbours, exactly?
Three pieces decide that. Partition splits the rows into independent groups, like a group by, but without collapsing anything.
Order fixes the sequence inside each group, which is what makes the word neighbour mean something.
And the frame is the slice a function actually sees for one current row. Most of the surprises in this topic live in that third piece.
There are three ways to count a frame, and the difference only shows when rows tie. Look at the two orders with the same timestamp, outlined in red.
Rows counts physical rows. It stops at the current row and does not care that another row is tied with it.
Range counts by value. Rows that tie on the ordering key are peers, and a frame that reaches one peer reaches all of them together.
Hold that difference, because the next question is a trap.
Four orders: a hundred, fifty, twenty five, and ten. The fifty and the twenty five share a timestamp.
You ask for a running total ordered by time, and you write no frame at all.
What do the two tied rows show?
answer: Both show a hundred and seventy five.
With no frame written, the default is the range kind, and it runs to the last peer of the current row. Each tied row is a peer of the other, so each includes both amounts.
A hundred and fifty and a hundred and seventy five would be the answer you wanted, one row at a time, but that needs a different frame. And the amounts alone are not totals.

lines: Watch the totals appear as the bracket moves. The first order shows a hundred.
Then the bracket reaches the tie. It cannot stop at the fifty, because the twenty five is a peer, so the frame jumps to include both.
That is why the total steps once per distinct timestamp, not once per row.
Nothing is broken. This is exactly what the default promises, and it is rarely what anyone expects.
So say what you meant. Break the tie with a unique second key, and ask for rows.
Now the bracket moves one physical row at a time, and each row advances the total by itself: a hundred, a hundred and fifty, a hundred and seventy five, a hundred and eighty five.
Notice that both changes are needed. Rows alone, without a unique key, leaves the order among tied rows undefined, so which one goes first can change from run to run.
The third mode counts in peer groups. Look at the dashed outlines: four orders, but only three groups.
One group back means one tie group, however many rows it holds. So the offset follows the data, not the row count.
Use it when ties are meaningful, for example all events in the same second, and you want the previous second as a unit.
Sometimes you want to leave something out of the frame. That is what exclude is for.
Excluding the current row gives you the others. Excluding the group drops the row and its peers. Excluding ties drops the peers but keeps the row itself.
The classic use is a comparison to the average of everything else, without the row itself leaking into the average.
If several functions share a definition, repeating it is asking for drift.
Name the window once, and refer to it by name. Every call is then guaranteed to use exactly the same frame.
One subtlety: naming it and adding to it are different. Adding is refused if the named window already has a frame.
Here is a rule that surprises people. A window function cannot contain another window function.
Look at the red box. Putting a running total inside a rank is refused outright.
The reason is order of evaluation: the inner one has to produce a value before the outer one can read it.
So give it a boundary. Compute the first in an inner query, and let the outer query read the result as an ordinary column.
Apply it. You want to rank customers by a running total, and the running total is itself a window.
How do you write that?
answer: Stage it. Compute the running total in an inner query, then rank that column in the outer one.
Nesting the two in one expression is rejected, and two over clauses on one call does not exist. It can certainly be done, which rules out the last option.

lines: Take three habits from this.
If ties can happen, do not trust the default frame. Add a unique key to the ordering, and write the rows frame out.
Name any definition shared by more than one call. And when you need a window of a window, stage it with a CTE.
Defining the neighbourhood is one job. Next: what the engine actually does, physically, to deliver an answer for every single row in it.
Two checks. First, one of the three frame modes pays no attention to ties.
Which one?
answer: It counts physical rows, so peers make no difference. Range and groups both work through peers, in different ways.

lines: Second check. An ordering is given, and no frame clause.
Which rows does the frame include?
answer: From the start of the partition up to the last peer of the current row.
Only the current row would be the rows frame, and the whole partition is what you get with no ordering at all.
